Why agentic security is its own subject

Traditional application security assumes software follows explicit control flow. Agents interpret untrusted content, choose tools, hold memory and delegate work, so the security boundary moves.

Intent is not authority

A natural-language request must never become an implicit grant of permission.

Prompt injection is a control-plane attack

Instructions can arrive in documents, email, web pages, tool output, code comments and images.

Tool access turns errors into impact

A mistaken or manipulated plan can move money, change systems, run code or disclose data.

Identity and delegation are dynamic

Users, agents, sub-agents, service accounts and tools form authority chains that change at run time.

Memory and retrieval persist

Poisoned context can shape later sessions long after the original interaction.

Multi-agent systems correlate failure

Trust propagates, permissions compound and a small compromise can cascade.

Assurance must be continuous

Model, prompt, tool, policy and data changes alter behaviour, so controls have to be measured again.

Design thesis. Minimise agency, constrain authority, isolate execution, authenticate every actor, validate every consequential action, treat model-visible data as untrusted, and keep measuring whether the controls work.

How learning is assessed

Knowledge is necessary, not sufficient

Every level combines blueprint-balanced knowledge items with observed lab or design work. A knowledge score alone never earns a level.

Evidence you can inspect

Each lesson ends in an artefact that goes into one evolving portfolio, the Secure Agentic Enterprise Dossier, so assessors review what you built.

Controls must fail closed

Practical tasks include negative tests: the control has to refuse the attack, not just permit the intended use.

Unseen forms and item control

Practice items and assessment items are separate pools. Assessment items are exposure-tracked and retired.

Separated decisions

The people who teach a level do not decide whether a candidate meets the standard. Appeals go to a reviewer who did not assess the candidate.

Design benchmark, not a claim

ISO/IEC 17024:2026 guides the design of the scheme. Intellica makes no accreditation or conformity claim.

How the academy works

Hands on at every level

Each lesson in the course has a lab step that builds part of one security design for an agent system you know, and checks it with tools you run yourself, not only quizzes.

Free lessons first

Lessons 1 and 5 are free to open, so you can judge the teaching before you decide.

Join at your level

Start at Level 1, or take the placement check: 48 original practice questions, 8 per level, scored in your browser. Nothing is stored or sent.

What the academy is not

  • The academy maps to public frameworks and exam objectives. It is independent of those bodies, is not a training provider for any external exam and does not promise an exam result.
  • The placement check is a self-check made of original practice questions. It is not an assessment and does not count towards any credential.
  • An Intellica certificate shows that you completed an Intellica course and met its published rule. Intellica’s own assessed credentials for the six levels are planned, not available.
  • Lessons marked planned are not written yet. They are listed on the roadmap with the gap each one closes.

What it is built on

Public standards and exam objectives are used as references and mappings, and every source is dated.

The curriculum maps to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, OWASP AISVS, MITRE ATLAS, the NIST AI RMF and the public objectives of external exams such as GIAC GAIPS. See the source register and the GAIPS mapping.

Reviewed 2026-11-24. Intellica is independent of GIAC, ISC2, ISACA, CompTIA, CSA, IAPP, OWASP, MITRE and NIST. Mappings show how our lessons relate to published objectives. They are not an affiliation, an approval or a prediction of any exam result.
